### Why Python for Data Analysis?

.font75[
.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("face-smile", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Easy to learn syntax**

Readable, expressive syntax with strong typing conventions. Python is the #1 language in data science, ML, and AI research &mdash; knowing it opens every modern data role.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("battery-full", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Batteries included**

NumPy (vectorized math), pandas (tabular data), matplotlib/seaborn (visualization), scikit-learn (ML), TensorFlow/PyTorch (deep learning) &mdash; the complete data science stack.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("globe", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Broad usage**

Netflix uses Python for recommendation algorithms, Spotify for music analysis, NASA for mission data pipelines, and Instagram for backend infrastructure.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("users", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Large community**

The largest data science community worldwide. Stack Overflow, GitHub, Kaggle, and Hugging Face are all Python-first &mdash; help is always one search away, including from AI coding agents.
]
]
]

### Why Jupyter in This Class?

.pull-left[.font85[
- Jupyter implements the **literate programming paradigm**: code, output, and narrative coexist in one document &mdash; making analysis self-documenting and reproducible. Required by many research journals and data competitions.

- To add a text cell in Jupyter, switch the cell to **"Markdown" mode** and you can write descriptions in plain English (and even include math or images).

- Markdown supports LaTeX math, hyperlinks, images, and tables &mdash; a single `.ipynb` file can contain a complete analysis from data loading to conclusions, shareable as a PDF or web page.
]]

### What is Pandas?

.font85[
.content-box-blue[
**pandas** is the standard Python library for tabular data &mdash; built on NumPy arrays for speed. The primary data structure (DataFrame) was inspired by R's `data.frame`.
]

**Core EDA workflow:** load &rarr; inspect dtypes &rarr; clean &rarr; transform &rarr; aggregate &rarr; visualize. pandas handles every step. Most real-world datasets live in DataFrames first.

**Main data structures:**

- **Series:** 1D labeled array. Each column of a DataFrame is a Series. Supports vectorized operations &mdash; no loops needed.

- **DataFrame:** 2D labeled table with a row index and named columns. Think SQL table or Excel sheet &mdash; with the full power of Python.
]

---
### Analysis Steps: The 5-Step EDA Workflow in Python

.font80[
<div class="chev-flow">
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("download", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>1. Import libraries</strong><br>
    pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, seaborn. Every analysis starts here.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("file-csv", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>2. Load the dataset</strong><br>
    <code>pd.read_csv()</code>. Check <code>df.shape</code> immediately &mdash; does the row count match what you expect?</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("magnifying-glass", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>3. Data audit</strong><br>
    <code>df.head()</code>, <code>df.dtypes</code>, <code>df.info()</code>, <code>df.describe()</code>. Flag type mismatches and missing values before any analysis.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("circle-question", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>4. Answer specific questions</strong><br>
    Compute statistics (mean, median, groupby, value_counts). Each answer raises new questions &mdash; that's EDA.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("chart-column", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>5. Visualize</strong><br>
    Histograms for distributions, bar charts for categories, scatter plots for relationships. Always interpret shape, not just numbers.</p>
  </div>
</div>
]

### Step 1: Import Libraries

.pull-left[
**Import:**

#### `r fontawesome::fa("chart-line", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; matplotlib for plotting

]

.pull-right[
**How can we import them?**

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

.font90[
- We use the `import` function and provide the package name.

### Step 5: Visualization &mdash; Basic Plotting in Python (Matplotlib)

.font90[
- Python has multiple plotting libraries.
- The foundational one is **Matplotlib**, which provides low-level plotting functions.
- Let's import the package as `plt`:
]

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

--

.content-box-blue[
.font90[**How is miles per gallon distributed?** A histogram shows the distribution of a continuous numeric variable by grouping values into "bins" (ranges) and plotting bars for the count of observations in each bin.]
]

---
### Histogram of MPG in Python

.pull-left[
```python
plt.hist(df["mpg"], bins=10,
         color='skyblue',
         edgecolor='black')
plt.title("Distribution of Car MPG")
plt.xlabel("Miles per Gallon (MPG)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Cars")
plt.show()
```

.font80[
- `plt.hist(df["mpg"], bins=10)` creates a histogram with **10 intervals (bins)**.
- `color='skyblue', edgecolor='black'` styles the bars (similar to R).
- `plt.title`, `plt.xlabel`, `plt.ylabel`: add title and axis labels as in R.
- `plt.show()` displays the plot &mdash; good practice, especially in scripts.
]
]

.pull-right[
```{r img53, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="90%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}

# Plot the image

```
]

---
### Histogram &mdash; Interpretation

.pull-left[.font75[
- This histogram shows MPG **distribution shape** &mdash; each bar is a bin (value range), height is count. Shape tells you things no single statistic can: skewness, clusters, gaps, outliers.

- This is **right-skewed** &mdash; the right tail is longer. Mean (21.3) &gt; Median (20.0) &mdash; a classic signature. A few fuel-efficient imports pull the mean upward.

- The **mode bin is 15&ndash;20 MPG**. Ask: would you have predicted this shape from the mean alone? This is why visualization precedes modeling.

- **Try `bins=5` vs `bins=20`.** Fewer bins over-smooth; too many bins show noise. The choice of bins is an analytical decision, not a technical one.
]]

.pull-right[

### Reflection: R vs. Python

.font70[
.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("gauge-high", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Speed of Development**

R: one-line `summary()` with quartiles for all columns. Python: `df.describe()` + `df.dtypes` separate. For statistical analysis, R often has fewer keystrokes. For ML pipelines, Python wins.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("chart-column", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Visualization**

R's ggplot2 (grammar of graphics) is more principled &mdash; every chart is data + aesthetics + geometry. Python's matplotlib is more imperative but seaborn wraps it more cleanly for statistical plots.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("plug", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Integration**

Python integrates with APIs, web services, databases, ML frameworks, and cloud platforms. R integrates tightly with academic publishing (R Markdown, Quarto). Most data teams use both.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("graduation-cap", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Learning Curve**

R: function-centric (everything is a function call). Python: object-oriented (methods called on objects). Both are learnable &mdash; the concepts transfer; only the syntax differs.
]
]
]

---
### Being Bilingual in Data Science

.pull-left[
```{r img67, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/67-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font75[
**`r fontawesome::fa("shuffle", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Flexibility** &mdash; pandas + matplotlib for quick EDA; ggplot2 + dplyr for statistical reporting; scikit-learn (Python) for ML; Stan/brms (R) for Bayesian modeling. The question isn't which is better &mdash; it's which is right for *this* job.

**`r fontawesome::fa("users", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Collaboration** &mdash; most industry data teams are bilingual. A Python-only analyst who can't read an R script will miss insights from 50% of the academic literature. Vice versa for R-only analysts.

**`r fontawesome::fa("briefcase", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Career Advantage** &mdash; top data science job postings increasingly list both. Kaggle and academic research often require Python; pharma, finance, and social science research often require R.

**`r fontawesome::fa("arrows-rotate", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Learning Transfer** &mdash; data frames, vectorization, split-apply-combine, and the grammar of graphics are language-agnostic concepts. Learn them once; apply them everywhere &mdash; including in coding agents.
]]

---
### R vs. Python: Syntax Comparison

.font80[

| Task | R Syntax | Python (pandas) Syntax |
|------|----------|------------------------|
| Reading data | `read.csv("file.csv")` | `pd.read_csv("file.csv")` |
| Viewing data | `head(df)` | `df.head()` |
| Summary stats | `summary(df)` | `df.describe()` |
| Accessing column | `df$col` | `df["col"]` |
| Mean of column | `mean(df$col)` | `df["col"].mean()` |
| Frequency count | `table(df$col)` | `df["col"].value_counts()` |
| Installing packages | `install.packages("pkg")` | `pip install pkg` (in terminal) |
| Call package from library | `library(pkg)` | `import pkg` |

]

Histograms (distributions), bar charts (categories), scatter plots (relationships). Interpret shape, not just numbers.

# Coding Agents for Python-Based EDA `r top_icon("robot")`

---
### Python + Coding Agent: EDA Workflow

.font80[An agent can execute your entire EDA pipeline &mdash; **but only if you give it precise, analytical instructions**:]

.pull-left[
.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("xmark", fill = "#D55E00")` Weak**

"Analyze the data."

&rarr; Agent produces arbitrary outputs with no analytical focus.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-green[
**`r fontawesome::fa("check", fill = "#009E73")` Strong**

"Load car_data.csv. Run `df.shape`, `df.dtypes`, `df.describe()`, and `df.isnull().sum()`. Report any columns with null values or dtypes that look wrong. Then compute mean and median for all numerical columns and flag where they differ by more than 10%."
]
]

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

.font75[
**The 4-step agent loop for EDA:** (1) You set the analytical question. (2) Agent writes and runs pandas code. (3) You evaluate the output &mdash; does it answer the question? Are dtypes right? Is the sample size expected? (4) You iterate with follow-up questions.

**Key risk:** agents confidently produce wrong code. Always cross-check &mdash; `df.shape` should match the expected row count, `df.describe()` min/max should be physically plausible.
]

---
### Seaborn: Statistical Visualization in Python

.font85[
**Why seaborn over matplotlib for statistical plots:** matplotlib is imperative (you specify every detail). **seaborn** is declarative &mdash; built on matplotlib, it generates statistically-informed plots in one line.

**Key seaborn functions for EDA:**

```python
sns.histplot(df, x="mpg", kde=True)               # histogram + KDE overlay
sns.boxplot(df, x="foreign", y="price")           # compare distributions across groups
sns.scatterplot(df, x="weight", y="mpg", hue="foreign")  # scatter colored by category
sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True)                # correlation matrix at once
```
]

--

### Chapter 4: What You Can Do Now

.font75[
**Python environment:**

- Set up Jupyter (Anaconda or Google Colab) and run the 5-step EDA workflow from import to visualization.

**Data analysis in Python:**

- Load CSV with `pd.read_csv()`. Audit with `df.shape`, `df.dtypes`, `df.describe()`, `df.isnull().sum()`. Flag mismatches before computing statistics.
- Compute mean, median, std, IQR, `value_counts()`, and `groupby()` aggregations. Interpret when mean and median diverge and why.
- Create matplotlib histograms, bar charts, and scatter plots. Generate seaborn statistical plots (histplot with KDE, boxplot, heatmap).

**Bilingual data science:**

- Map equivalent operations between R and Python (`summary()` &harr; `describe()`, `$` &harr; `df["col"]`, `tapply()` &harr; `groupby()`). Know when to use each language.
- Direct a coding agent to perform full EDA in Python, evaluate its outputs critically, and iterate with precise analytical follow-up prompts.
]
